title: 2 Samuel 8:1–14
context: 2 Samuel 8 summarizes David’s military victories, which secured Israel’s borders and brought surrounding peoples under his rule. The chapter follows the covenant promise of chapter 7 and shows part of its fulfillment: God had said, “I will cause you to rest from all your enemies” (7:11). David defeats the Philistines, Moab, Hadadezer of Zobah, the Syrians of Damascus and Edom, and receives tribute and gifts, which he dedicates to the LORD. Twice the narrator says, “The LORD gave victory to David wherever he went” (8:6, 14). The account parallels 1 Chronicles 18, which differs in some names and numbers; the notes point out these differences plainly where they occur, without trying to settle them. The severe treatment of Moab (8:2) and the hamstringing of horses (8:4) are recorded without comment and are read here in the narrative’s own setting.

verses.text: After this, David struck the Philistines and subdued them; and David took the bridle of the mother city out of the hand of the Philistines.
verses.arminianNotes: David strikes the Philistines, subdues them, and takes “the bridle of the mother city” out of their hand. Arminian readers note that the long Philistine threat, which troubled Israel since Saul’s day, is finally broken under David, the fulfillment of God’s purpose for his anointed king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase “the bridle of the mother city” is unusual; the parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:1 reads “took Gath and its towns.” The text does not explain the difference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the beginning of God’s promised rest for Israel through David (7:11), and neither finds a doctrinal question in it.

verses.text: He defeated Moab, and measured them with the line, making them to lie down on the ground; and he measured two lines to put to death, and one full line to keep alive. The Moabites became servants to David, and brought tribute.
verses.arminianNotes: David defeats Moab and measures the captives with a line, putting two lines to death and keeping one line alive. Arminian readers acknowledge the severity of this act, recorded without comment by the narrator. The text gives no reason for it, and one is not supplied here. Moab had once sheltered David’s parents (1 Samuel 22:3–4), which makes the account all the more sobering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse soberly, noting that the narrator neither praises nor condemns the act and that the parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:2 does not mention it. Some readers recall Balaam’s oracle of a scepter that would “strike through the corners of Moab” (Numbers 24:17). Shared ground: both traditions refuse to speculate beyond the text and read it within the harsh realities of warfare in Israel’s history, not as a model.

verses.text: David also struck Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his dominion at the River.
verses.arminianNotes: David strikes Hadadezer, king of Zobah, “as he went to recover his dominion at the River.” Arminian readers note that David’s campaigns extend Israel’s influence far to the north, toward the boundaries promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18). The parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:3 names the river as the Euphrates.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the promise of land “to the great river, the river Euphrates” (Genesis 15:18) begins to be realized under David, and more fully under Solomon (1 Kings 4:24). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing God fulfilling his ancient promises through David’s reign, and both note that it is not always clear whose dominion is meant in the phrase.

verses.text: David took from him one thousand seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand footmen. David hamstrung the chariot horses, but reserved enough of them for one hundred chariots.
verses.arminianNotes: David takes “one thousand seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand footmen,” hamstrings the chariot horses, and keeps enough for one hundred chariots. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:4 reads “one thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen.” Arminian readers note the difference plainly without trying to resolve it here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that hamstringing horses had precedent in Joshua 11:6, where the LORD commanded it, and that Deuteronomy 17:16 warns the king not to “multiply horses to himself.” The act disabled the enemy’s chariot force. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly in its own setting, and both recall Psalm 20:7: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.”

verses.text: When the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck twenty two thousand men of the Syrians.
verses.arminianNotes: When the Syrians of Damascus come to help Hadadezer, David strikes twenty-two thousand of them. Arminian readers note that David’s victories continue as other nations ally against him. The coalition cannot prevail against the king whom God has established.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Syrians’ intervention only expands David’s victory. God’s promise to cut off David’s enemies (7:9) is being fulfilled. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the summary of David’s victories, and both see in it God’s faithfulness to his word.

verses.text: Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus; and the Syrians became servants to David, and brought tribute. The LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verses.arminianNotes: David places garrisons in Syria, which becomes subject and pays tribute. “The LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.” Arminian readers note that the narrator credits the victories to the LORD, not to David’s skill alone. David’s success is God’s gift, and the refrain guards against reading the chapter as a celebration of human power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the narrator’s theological summary, repeated in 8:14, which frames the whole chapter: victory belongs to the LORD. Shared ground: both traditions read the refrain as common ground, showing that God fulfills his promises through David and that all success comes from him (compare 2 Samuel 5:10, “the LORD, the God of Armies, was with him”).

verses.text: David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadadezer, and brought them to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: David takes Hadadezer’s servants’ shields of gold and brings them to Jerusalem. Arminian readers note that the spoils of victory are brought to David’s capital, symbolizing the transfer of power and wealth to Israel under God’s blessing. Jerusalem, newly taken, gains in honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the gold shields, brought to Jerusalem, prepare for the dedication of spoils to the LORD in 8:11. Jerusalem is becoming the center of God’s kingdom on earth. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the narrative of God’s blessing on David’s reign, and neither finds a doctrinal question in it.

verses.text: From Betah and from Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, King David took a great quantity of bronze.
verses.arminianNotes: From Betah and Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, David takes a great quantity of bronze. Arminian readers note the wealth that comes to Israel through God’s blessing. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:8 names the cities Tibhath and Cun and adds that Solomon used the bronze for the temple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the Chronicler’s detail that this bronze was later used to make “the bronze sea, the pillars, and the vessels of bronze” (1 Chronicles 18:8), linking David’s victories with the temple his son would build (7:13). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that God’s provision through David served the future worship of his house.

verses.text: When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had struck all the army of Hadadezer,
verses.arminianNotes: Toi, king of Hamath, hears that David has struck all the army of Hadadezer. Arminian readers note that David’s victories make him known among the nations. News of God’s work through David spreads, and other kings take notice and must decide how to respond to Israel’s king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the reaction of Toi shows the effect of God’s promise to make David’s name great (7:9). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as setting up Toi’s embassy, and both see in it the growing recognition of David’s kingdom among surrounding peoples. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:9 spells the name Tou.

verses.text: then Toi sent Joram his son to King David to greet him and to bless him, because he had fought against Hadadezer and struck him; for Hadadezer had wars with Toi. Joram brought with him vessels of silver, vessels of gold, and vessels of bronze.
verses.arminianNotes: Toi sends his son Joram to greet and bless David, with gifts of silver, gold and bronze, because Hadadezer had been Toi’s enemy. Arminian readers note that peaceful relations follow David’s victories. Not every nation is subdued by force; some seek friendship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the gifts from Toi anticipate the nations bringing tribute to the son of David, a theme developed in later Scripture. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:10 names the son Hadoram. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the widening influence of David’s kingdom under God’s blessing.

verses.text: King David also dedicated these to the LORD, with the silver and gold that he dedicated of all the nations which he subdued—
verses.arminianNotes: David dedicates Toi’s gifts to the LORD, along with the silver and gold from all the nations he subdued. Arminian readers note David’s devotion. He does not keep the spoils for himself but offers them to the LORD, acknowledging that the victories were God’s.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David’s dedication of the spoils is consistent with his earlier desire to build God a house (7:2). Though not permitted to build the temple, he gathers materials for it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an act of worship and gratitude, recognizing God as the source of all David’s success.

verses.text: of Syria, of Moab, of the children of Ammon, of the Philistines, of Amalek, and of the plunder of Hadadezer, son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
verses.arminianNotes: The dedicated spoils come “of Syria, of Moab, of the children of Ammon, of the Philistines, of Amalek, and of the plunder of Hadadezer.” Arminian readers note the breadth of David’s victories, which cover Israel’s traditional enemies on every side. Everything taken from them is offered to the LORD, not kept as personal wealth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the list includes Ammon and Amalek, not mentioned earlier in this chapter, showing that the summary gathers David’s campaigns from across his reign. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:11 lists Edom in place of Syria. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a summary of God’s victories through David, and both note the parallel’s different wording plainly.

verses.text: David earned a reputation when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand men of the Syrians in the Valley of Salt.
verses.arminianNotes: David earns a reputation when he returns from striking down “eighteen thousand men of the Syrians in the Valley of Salt.” Arminian readers note that the parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:12 says Abishai struck eighteen thousand of the Edomites in the Valley of Salt. The WEB text of 2 Samuel reads “Syrians,” and the next verse turns to Edom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the difference plainly without resolving it here. The verse itself links the victory with David’s growing reputation, in keeping with God’s promise of a great name. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing God’s gift of a great name to David (7:9), and both refrain from speculation about the textual differences.

verses.text: He put garrisons in Edom. Throughout all Edom, he put garrisons, and all the Edomites became servants to David. The LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verses.arminianNotes: David puts garrisons throughout Edom, and all the Edomites become his servants. “The LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.” Arminian readers note the repetition of the refrain from 8:6, which frames the chapter and credits David’s success to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the subjugation of Edom recalls the ancient word to Rebekah that the older would serve the younger (Genesis 25:23), and they emphasize that the refrain frames all of David’s victories as God’s work. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing refrain as common ground, teaching that victory and blessing come from the LORD.
